name: archive_probe
description: Say what an archive or a document shows about its own protection, and what it does not. ZIP: structural, read by this tool from the bytes: the End Of Central Directory record (the one whose comment ends the file; another sound End record, in a comment, after the archive, or of an archive that lies wholly before the one that ends the file (a second archive appended; looked for in the last 64 KiB), is named, the answer is partial and protected is not false), the Zip64 end record wherever a Zip64 locator sits before it (whatever the End record says, as zipfile follows it), and each central directory entry (empty and self-extracting archives included): per-member encryption, the WinZip AES extra field, DOS times with their raw words and no zone; a name that is not valid UTF-8 is shown escaped and does not hide the other members. 7-Zip: listed through the installed 7z (bounded, no password prompt; it is ended at the clock, on a signal and, on Linux, when the tool is killed, but a program 7z itself started is not, and on macOS a killed tool leaves its 7z) where there is one, giving the members, each one's encrypted flag and whether the header is encrypted; the start header is read and its checksums checked, and a byte search is kept as a hint only when 7z is absent or cannot read the file. RAR: identified, protection not determined. PDF and OLE/Office: a heuristic byte search for markers, reported with offsets, never as 'not encrypted' and never as a verdict (the structural document reader is not provided by this pack). Whether member names are readable is a finding separate from whether the data is encrypted. Nothing is extracted. What is loaded is bounded by max_metadata_bytes whatever the file's own headers declare: a ZIP whose central directory is declared larger than the bound (in the End record or the Zip64 record), larger than the file, or with more entries than the bound holds at 46 bytes each is not listed and says so; the directory is read in blocks, so memory does not follow its size. A PDF or an OLE file is searched whole, in a linear pass (bytes_searched and search_complete say so), because a PDF's marker sits at its end. The tool has its own clock (max_seconds, default 100, below the timeout of 120): at it, or on SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP, it ends the 7z it started and answers once (status partial or interrupted, exit 128 + the signal). The clock is read for every ZIP entry and every 7z header string, and every mapped part of a file is read through the descriptor before it is used; a read that has not returned five seconds after the clock (a file on a volume or share that is not available) ends the tool with one answer, status partial, exit 0. The stop is the clock's, not the work's: the timer stays armed while the answer is sealed, so an answer too large to seal in that time is replaced by the short partial one, and a page fault or a read that sits in the system (a dead share) cannot be ended until the call returns. Every answer carries status and status_basis. SENSITIVE: member names, 7-Zip header strings, the 7z diagnostics and the path are evidence text. A part of one shaped like an identifier or a secret (a run of 10 digits or more, letters and digits of 8 or more, grouped digits, a recovery password, password=... , user-info, vendor tokens) is replaced by a marker in the answer and in every file it names (names_withheld counts them), the rest of the name stays; a second check of the output replaces what the first let through and makes the answer partial. Withholding is by shape, measured on random draws per shape planted in a member name or path (rates, not guarantees). Printed whole in 0 of 1,000 draws: hexadecimal ids of 16, 32 and 64, numbers of 10 digits or more, recovery passwords written with dashes, spaces, dots, underscores, no separator or one to three of any other characters between the groups (an en dash, a comma, a colon, a pipe, a tab), also when the groups are cut at the separators of the path (123456-123456/123456-...), full-width, split by invisible characters, or with one decimal digit glued to the first or last group, AWS access key ids, password= and api_key: assignments, user-info, 4x4 groups of capitals and digits joined by - or ., letters and digits of 8, 9, 12, 16 or 40 characters that hold a capital, a small letter and a digit, and a full-width id. Printed whole in some draws: uniform draws of letters and digits (every character as likely a capital, a small letter or a digit as any other) of 8 characters about 2.5%, of 9 about 2%, of 12 about 1%, of 16 about 0.6%, of 24 at most 0.1% and of 40 none; random lowercase letters and digits of 8 about 7%, of 12 about 2.4%, of 16 about 0.4%; 24 random letters 1.5% to 2.6%; a 16-character base32 id 2.2% to 3.4% (by alphabet); four groups of four lowercase hexadecimal digits joined by underscores 4% to 9% (by how the draws are made); an id of 12 or 16 characters whose letters are half Cyrillic or Greek look-alikes about 1%. NOT recognised, by design, and printed whole: an identifier of 7 characters or fewer, a number of 9 digits or fewer, a lowercase-only run of up to 22 letters (it reads as a word), an all-capital letters-only run of any length, three groups of four or five capitals and digits joined by - or . (a rule for them would also withhold upper-case constants such as OpenSSL manual page names), a recovery password cut by anything other than a separator or with a letter in it or glued to it (the groups then show), a ten-digit number written 3-3-4, an e-mail-like lowercase string, and a secret of any other shape; a file whose secrets matter is read in a job run with secret_output: true. What the rule is given is bounded: a string of more than 4096 characters (as written or after folding), a path of more than 8192, or a string with a / and a run of more than 256 name characters is withheld whole as '<text too long to judge withheld>' and not judged (the slowest string inside the bound that a search found took 0.13 CPU s). The output check, which reads every printed string once more, is narrower than the rule: with the rule removed it replaces recovery passwords (full-width ones too), AWS ids, password= values, PEM headers, user-info, hexadecimal of 16 digits or more and runs of 24 or more characters that flip between letters and digits, and it lets through numbers of 10 to 20 digits, ids of up to 23 characters, some base64 (about one in five of 32 bytes), every recovery password whose groups are joined by anything but a hyphen, underscore, dot, space or nothing, and every recovery password cut over the components of a path (the first layer alone holds those). The rule also changes names that are not secrets: of the file names of a documents tree 6.9% have a part withheld (10-digit timestamps, UUIDs) and 0.6% of its directories, of an application tree 16% and 3.1% (a word with a digit inside, such as libmp3lame, is withheld in part).

path.description: A ZIP, 7-Zip, RAR, PDF or OLE document

limit.description: Members (or 7-Zip header strings) shown inline (default 200); all of them are counted, and when there are more the whole list is written as JSON Lines and named in all_results

max_metadata_bytes.description: The most container metadata to load or search: a ZIP central directory, a 7-Zip header (default 33554432, at least 4096). A ZIP whose central directory is declared larger (in either end record), larger than the file, or with more entries than this holds at 46 bytes each is not listed and says so. It does not bound the search of a PDF or an OLE file, which is always whole

max_seconds.description: The tool's own time limit in seconds (default 100, 1 to 110; the manifest's timeout is 120). At it the 7z is ended and the answer says what was not read; a read that has not returned five seconds later ends the tool with one partial answer
